En 2024, trois jeunes de moins de 16 ans: In 2024, three young people under the age of 16 lost their lives to gun violence in Saint-Léonard. In response to the alarming growth of this phenomenon, a citizens' forum was launched in the same borough. The residents behind the initiative want to understand, prevent and propose solutions, while highlighting the resources that already exist.
Cet article fait suite à « Nos quartiers: This article follows “Our Neighbourhoods, Our Voices: Parent-Child Dialogue to Prevent Gun Violence.” This time, I look at the solutions available to parents whose child is already caught in this spiral.
Parmi les initiatives présentées, les at: Among the initiatives presented, the Espace-Parents workshops play a key role. They support parents who are new to the country so they can better understand cultural differences and maintain a healthy relationship with their children. Because the same pattern often comes up: exclusion, lack of bearings, a feeling of abandonment – all factors that can lead to gun violence.

<strong><em>En 2024, trois jeunes de Sai: In 2024, three young people from Saint-Léonard died in connection with gun violence. Mehdi Moussaoui and a 16-year-old lost their lives in a car crash after shooting at two drivers. Last September, 14-year-old Mohamed-Yanis Seghouani was found dead in Frampton, near the hideout of a Hells Angels puppet club. For many parents, fear takes over: how do you keep your child from ending up there? The anxiety is even greater among immigrant families, who left everything behind in the hope of a better future for their children. But faced with isolation, integration difficulties and a lack of bearings, some young people become prey for gang recruiters, who dangle the promise of “easy” money in front of them. What resources exist to prevent this from happening? What can be done when prevention is no longer enough? A report.
Samedi 22 février 2025, 9 h 40. Dans la: Saturday, February 22, 2025, 9:40 a.m. In the main library of Saint-Léonard, about a hundred residents, elected officials and community workers are seated at tables for the second edition of the Forum Citoyen, organized by Concertation Saint-Léonard. The goal is to discuss, understand and find solutions to the rise in gun violence. The diversity of the participants reflects how serious the issue is: urban safety concerns every generation and every community.
<strong>« Il faut sortir de l’isolement,: “You have to break out of isolation, go get help”
Samira*, la cinquantaine, est visiblemen: Samira*, in her fifties, is visibly moved as she takes her place in front of the audience. She introduces herself as a mother and a former trial lawyer in her country of origin. Her family has been touched by gun violence, and she has come to share her story. Her voice trembles, but she is determined to speak.
« Nous sommes arrivés au Canada il y a c: “We arrived in Canada five years ago. My husband and I chose to come here for our children's future, but the reality of settling in this new country overwhelmed us,” Samira says softly. “We're asylum seekers, so we had to deal with endless paperwork. My husband was working non-stop, and at the same time, we found out my daughter had a brain tumour. Meanwhile, my 15-year-old son was left on his own, and on top of that, he was being made fun of at school.”
Son regard balaie la salle. « Certains p: Her gaze sweeps across the room. “Some parents forbid their children from spending time with newcomers, claiming we're synonymous with trouble,” Samira laments. “My son, shut out, became easy prey for gang recruiters. And I didn't see it coming…” the mother confides, a hint of guilt in her voice.
Quelque mois plus tard, l’adolescent est: A few months later, the teenager was arrested for robbing a convenience store with other kids his age. “People say it's newcomers who stir up trouble, but all the other kids he was with are Québécois,” she points out.
« Encore aujourd’hui, je peine à croire: “Even today, I can hardly believe he could have done that. I never imagined he could end up in that kind of situation. Maybe that's the real problem… believing our children aren't capable of the worst.” A heavy silence falls over the room. About a hundred people are listening to her without making a sound.
« Mais moi, j’ai refusé de l’abandonner,: “But I refused to give up on him,” she continues. “I looked for help. Often, in our communities, we'd rather stay quiet out of fear of being judged. But we have to realize that what people will say isn't what matters most – it's our child we need to help!”
Face à cette situation, elle se tourne v: Faced with this situation, she turned to youth protection services, the Direction de la protection de la jeunesse (DPJ), for help. “In six months, they did remarkable work. Truly, I'm grateful to them from the bottom of my heart,” Samira insists. “Today, my son is 20, he's awaiting trial, he's going to take responsibility for his mistakes – and I'm supporting him. He has to be a good citizen now. He's still a human being. He can do wrong just as he can do good.”
Des mains se lèvent dans la salle, plusi: Hands go up in the room, several making the shaka sign as a show of support. Then a round of applause breaks out. Robenson, a DPJ worker, watches the scene, eyes wide. “It's the first time I've ever heard a parent say the DPJ did a good job. I almost want to go give her a hug!” he says, laughing, moved.
Le forum ne fait que commencer. Après le: The forum is only just getting started. After the testimonies, a panel of speakers, including police and community organizations, takes the floor. Among them is Dolis Rodriguez, who runs the Espace-Parents workshops at Accueil aux immigrants de l'est de Montréal (AIEM).
Elle insiste : « Les parents en contexte: She insists: “Parents in an immigration context need support to understand their children's challenges and adapt to the Quebec context.”
<strong>Être parent en contexte d’immigr: Being a parent in an immigration context
Des parents témoignent de leur reconnais: Parents express their gratitude for the Espace-Parents workshops on sticky notes. Courtesy: Dolis Rodriguez
Pour en apprendre davantage sur les atel: To learn more about the Espace-Parents workshops, La Converse meets Dolis Rodriguez a few days later in a bright office at AIEM. She welcomes us with a warm smile, her brown hair pulled back in a half-ponytail.
« Les parents arrivent ici avec l’espoir: “Parents arrive here hoping for a better future for their children. But integration is a shock. They find themselves without bearings, not knowing where to look for support,” the program head begins. Work, language, cultural differences and fear of judgment are among the factors that also keep some parents from asking for that help. “They think they're the only ones going through so many difficulties. But when they join a group and realize other families are living the same thing, everything changes. They see that they're not alone, that it's normal to have challenges,” explains Dolis Rodriguez, who was a psychologist before emigrating from Cuba.
C’est justement pour briser l’isolement: It's precisely to break adults' isolation that the Espace-Parents program was designed. It offers eight themed workshops, divided into two main modules: the first aims to understand the impact of immigration on the family and to present the resources available. The second, titled “Au cœur de mon enfant” (At the heart of my child), helps parents support their child through their integration.
L’intervenante l’assure : « Au Québec, d: The worker is adamant: “In Quebec, asking for help isn't frowned upon. Quite the opposite. Many parents think they have to handle everything alone, that accepting help means failing in their role. They tell themselves, ‘This is my child, I should be able to take care of this on my own.’” “But when you ignore a small problem, it gets worse. And by the time you finally look for help, it's sometimes too late,” she says.
<strong>Les codes sociaux changent, les: Social codes change, and so do relationships
Apprendre le français ou trouver un nouv: Learning French or finding a new job isn't enough to feel you belong in your new home. “It also means understanding social codes, which sometimes contradict what you already know,” M<sup>s</sup> Rodriguez continues. It's a culture shock that can reshape relationships within families for the worse.
Pour les enfants, l’école est évidemment: For children, school is obviously a place of learning… but also a place where family values get called into question. “At school, young people are encouraged to express their opinions, to ask questions. At home, according to certain traditions, respect means silence, you have to keep quiet; and if you ask questions, it means you're becoming rebellious… And then, unfortunately, parents become harsher with the child. They think, ‘Oh, what's going on since my child got here? He's becoming rude.’ And the young person is lost.”
Mais ce constat peut également être fait: But the same can be said of institutions, she adds. “I've seen parents called in to school because their child wouldn't look their teacher in the eye. Here, that's seen as a lack of respect. But in their culture, it's the complete opposite: lowering your gaze in front of an adult is a sign of respect.”
Au-delà des différences culturelles, un: Beyond cultural differences, another major issue complicates the parent-child relationship: the fear of the first culture being rejected. “Parents want to pass on their culture, but they also want their children to succeed here. How do you find the balance?”
Dans ses ateliers, l’intervenante insist: In her workshops, the worker stresses one essential point: a child shouldn't have to choose between their new Québécois identity and their roots. “We give them tools to value the mother tongue without imposing it, to share moments around traditions without making them oppressive. What matters is that the child loves their heritage, not that they endure it.”
Le lien familial est crucial, insiste Do: The family bond is crucial, Dolis Rodriguez insists. “A young person who feels neither understood at home nor accepted outside becomes vulnerable. They'll look for a group to belong to. If it's not the family, it'll be somewhere else. Before, back in the home country, a child in conflict with their parents could turn to the extended family: cousins, aunts, grandparents… Here, if they break with their parents, they have no one left to talk to. That total isolation is dangerous.”
C’est pour éviter ce type de fracture qu: It's to prevent this kind of rupture that Espace-Parents exists: the workshops give families the means to remain a solid anchor in their children's lives. Finally, the Espace-Parents initiative also offers a presentation on the DPJ.
« Dans certaines communautés, la simple: “In some communities, just mentioning the DPJ is enough to cause anxiety,” M<sup>s</sup> Rodriguez continues. These fears, often fuelled by misconceptions, hold back many parents who would nonetheless like to ask for help.
C’est donc pour démystifier la DPJ qu’Es: So it's to demystify the DPJ that Espace-Parents offers an activity called “Mythes et réalités de la DPJ” (Myths and realities of the DPJ). The goal is to break down prejudices and help families better understand the institution's role.
Une des méthodes qui s’avèrent efficaces: One method that has proven effective is inviting DPJ workers to meet parents during the workshops, the worker explains. “That simple meeting often changes participants' perceptions.” Parents' reactions are often the same. “One mom once told me, ‘Oh, but they're just normal people after all!’” the young woman recounts, amused. “I don't know what they were expecting; yes, indeed, they're normal people.” Parents also notice that some DPJ workers themselves come from multicultural communities, which they see as a sign that they'll be understood.
« Dans leur pays d’origine, les autorité: “In their countries of origin, authorities are often seen as agents of repression. So meeting DPJ workers who take a gentler approach reassures them,” Dolis Rodriguez adds.
« ”On a signalé mon enfant à la DPJ ; do: “‘Someone reported my child to the DPJ, so I'm going to lose my kids!’ That's often what parents think, so they'd rather hide important information,” continues the worker, who encourages parents to be completely transparent with DPJ workers. “If a worker realizes a parent has hidden things, assessing the situation becomes more complicated. No, a report doesn't mean the child will be taken away from the family. Sometimes parents simply need resources the DPJ can point them to, but hiding things,” she warns once again, “risks making the assessment more complex.”
Dolis Rodriguez, elle, affirme n’avoir j: Dolis Rodriguez herself says she has never had to file a report.
Au cours de cette même activité où M​​<s: During the same activity in which Ms Rodriguez presents the “myths and realities” of the DPJ, participants are told that another widespread “myth” is that all children placed in youth centres become delinquents. The worker points out: “If a child is placed in a youth centre, it's because the assessment showed the young person couldn't stay with their family. But the ultimate goal isn't to separate the child from their parents. It's always the last resort…” However, an article published in Le Devoir portrayed the Cité-des-Prairies youth centre as a reflection of gun violence, where young people's safety is under even greater threat.
La DPJ est-elle alors réellement le dern: So is the DPJ really the last safety net?
René-André Brisebois, intervenant et che: René-André Brisebois, a practitioner and researcher at the Institut universitaire Jeunes en difficulté of the CIUSSS du Centre-Sud-de-l'Île-de-Montréal, responds: “Indeed, the DPJ can be a resource, although it isn't the first point of entry for help. Ideally, you step in as soon as the first difficulties appear, drawing on existing community resources.”
Toutefois, lorsque les comportements à r: However, when risky behaviour intensifies and a teenager sinks deeper into the spiral of violence, certain interventions become unavoidable. “They're not always pleasant solutions, but they're sometimes necessary to put an end to the situation and begin real support work,” he explains.
Mais quelles sont, concrètement, les éta: But what, concretely, are the steps in taking charge of a young person involved in a street gang or in gun violence? How do you help them cut ties with that environment? At the time of writing, the DPJ had not responded to our interview requests on these questions.
Ce qui est certain, c’est que l’accès au: What is certain is that access to resources remains a major issue. “The families who need help the most are often the ones who don't ask for it. They end up isolated, trapped in increasingly complex situations, which heightens their vulnerability,” Mr. Brisebois points out.
Et plus elles tardent à recevoir du sout: And the longer they wait to receive support, the worse the situation gets. “Support has to be proactive. We have to reach out to these families before it's too late,” he concludes.
Mais alors, comment rejoindre ces famill: So how do we reach these families, particularly newcomers, who may not know about the resources available to them? At Saint-Léonard's Forum Citoyen, several initiatives were raised, including training members of immigrant communities to support newcomers, known as “Femme-Relais” or “Homme-Relais” (liaison women or liaison men).
